310: "Adjacent" means directly next to something, typically sharing a side, edge, or border with it. Think of two things sitting right beside each other with nothing in between — that is the essence of "adjacent."

If your seat on a plane is adjacent to the window, your seat is right next to the window seat — not two rows ahead, not somewhere nearby, but directly beside it. If two houses are adjacent, they sit right next to each other, often sharing a wall or a fence line.

The word almost always describes a positional relationship — where something is relative to something else.

This is where many learners get it slightly wrong, so pay close attention.

"Adjacent" is stronger than just "near" or "close." "Near" is vague — it could mean a few feet or a few miles. "Adjacent," on the other hand, implies directly next to, with no meaningful gap or intervening thing between the two. If a café is near a library, it might be around the corner or down the street. If a café is adjacent to a library, it is right beside it — they likely share a wall or a property line.

That said, "adjacent" does not always mean the two things are physically touching. Two countries can be adjacent to each other even with a river running between them, as long as they sit right beside each other with no other country in between. The key idea is immediate neighborhood — one is the direct, closest neighbor of the other.
How it is used in a sentence

"Adjacent" is almost always followed by the preposition "to" when comparing two specific things:

  • The gym is adjacent to the swimming pool.
  • She moved to a room adjacent to mine.
  • The village is adjacent to a dense forest.

You can also use it before a noun on its own (without "to") when you are describing something as being a neighbor of whatever is already understood from context:

  • We sat in adjacent seats. (meaning our seats were right next to each other)
  • The adjacent building caught fire.
  • Open the adjacent file.

In geometry, "adjacent" is used with precision. Two adjacent angles are angles that share a common side and a common corner point. Two adjacent sides of a shape are sides that meet at a corner. In these contexts, "adjacent" strictly means directly connected or sharing something.

In mathematics, on a number line, the numbers 4 and 5 are adjacent because no whole number sits between them.

The word is also common in architecture, urban planning, law, and geography — anywhere precise spatial relationships matter.

In recent years, "adjacent" has taken on a looser, figurative meaning in everyday conversation and writing. People now use it to mean related to, or in the territory of, something — but not quite that thing itself.

For example:

  • "That movie is horror-adjacent" — meaning it feels like a horror film, shares some qualities with horror, but is not quite horror.
  • "His job is tech-adjacent" — meaning he does not work directly in technology, but his work is closely related to the tech world.
  • "That comment was rude-adjacent" — meaning it was not quite rude, but it was getting close to being rude.

This figurative use is informal and modern. It is widely understood, especially in casual writing and speech, but you would not use it in formal academic or professional writing.

Nearby — vague; just means somewhere in the general area, with no implication of being the direct next-door neighbor.

Close — describes proximity in a general sense, but again, vague. "Close" could mean many things depending on context.

Neighboring — very similar to "adjacent," and often interchangeable. However, "neighboring" tends to feel more natural with large-scale things like cities, countries, and communities (neighboring countries), while "adjacent" works equally well with both small things (adjacent seats) and large things (adjacent territories).

Beside — also very similar. The main difference is that "beside" is simpler and more conversational, while "adjacent" is more formal and precise.

Adjoining — almost identical to "adjacent," but with a stronger implication that the two things are physically connected or sharing a wall/border. Adjoining rooms share a door or a wall; adjacent rooms are right next to each other but may or may not share a wall.
A final way to picture it

Imagine a row of houses on a street: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. House 3 is adjacent to houses 2 and 4. It is not adjacent to houses 1 or 5 — those are nearby, but not directly next to it. Adjacent always means the immediate next-door neighbor, not just anything in the surrounding area.

Once you hold that image in your mind — the one directly beside, with nothing in between — you have the word completely understood.
311:
When two things adjoin, they are sitting directly next to each other and sharing a common boundary — a wall, a fence, a border line, or an edge. There is no gap between them. They are literally touching along one side.

Think of two puzzle pieces that fit together along one edge. They adjoin each other.
The single most important thing to understand

Adjoining ≠ merely nearby.

If two things are simply close to each other, they are not adjoining. To adjoin means the two things are in direct contact, sharing a physical boundary — a wall they both share, a fence line they both touch, or a border that belongs to both of them.

Two houses on the same street are near each other. Two houses that share a wall between them — like a semi-detached house — adjoin each other.
What kinds of things can adjoin?

Mostly physical spaces and areas:

  • Rooms — Two rooms in a building can adjoin if they share a wall and often a connecting door.
  • Buildings — A garage can adjoin a house if they share a common wall.
  • Properties / plots of land — Two plots adjoin if they share a boundary fence or line.
  • Countries / regions — France adjoins Germany because they share a national border. There is no other country in between them at that border.
  • Fields, gardens, parks — Any two areas of land that share an edge.

• "The bedroom adjoins the bathroom — you can walk directly from one into the other."
    → They share a wall, and there's a door connecting them.
  • "Our garden adjoins our neighbour's garden along the back wall."
    → The back wall is the shared boundary between the two gardens.
  • "Spain adjoins Portugal on its western side."
    → They share a national border along that side.
  • "The hotel room had an adjoining room, which was perfect for the family."
    → A second room directly connected to the first through a shared door in the shared wall.
  • "The two properties adjoin, so the owners often argue about the fence."
    → They share a boundary line, which is where the fence sits.
How it works in a sentence (without grammar jargon)

You can use "adjoin" in two natural ways:

Way 1 — One thing adjoins another thing:

"The kitchen adjoins the dining room."
(Kitchen → shares a boundary with → dining room)

Way 2 — Two things adjoin each other (or just "adjoin"):

"The two rooms adjoin." or "The two rooms adjoin each other."
(Both rooms share a boundary with the other)

Both ways are correct and common.

In real life, you will probably see the word adjoining (the adjective form) even more often than the verb itself. It means "directly next to and sharing a boundary with." It describes the thing that adjoins.

  • "An adjoining room" — a room that shares a wall/door with the room you're in.
  • "Adjoining fields" — fields that share a boundary edge.
  • "Adjoining properties" — land plots sharing a fence or boundary line.

You'll see "adjoining room" especially in hotels, where two rooms can be booked together and accessed through a shared door.

Near / close to: Just in the general vicinity. No direct contact required.

"The pharmacy is near the hospital" — they might be a street apart.
"The pharmacy adjoins the hospital" — they share a wall; they are in the same building complex.

Adjacent: Very similar to "adjoin," and often used interchangeably. However, "adjacent" can sometimes just mean "next to" without necessarily implying physical contact (e.g., "the adjacent seat" on a bus just means the seat beside you). "Adjoin" always implies a shared boundary — direct contact. So "adjoin" is the stricter, more precise word.

Abut: Practically a synonym of "adjoin." When one thing abuts another, it presses up against it along an edge. The two words are nearly identical in meaning. "Adjoin" is more common in general writing; "abut" appears more often in legal, architectural, and property contexts.

Border: Used more specifically for geographical areas — countries, states, regions. "France borders Spain" means the same as "France adjoins Spain." "Border" is more common in geographical and political contexts; "adjoin" is broader and works for rooms, buildings, and land too.
A mental image to lock it in

Imagine two sheets of paper lying flat on a table. You slide one sheet until its right edge touches the left edge of the other sheet perfectly — no gap, no overlap. At that moment, the two sheets adjoin each other. They share a common edge. That edge is their boundary.

Now scale that up: two rooms sharing a wall, two countries sharing a border, two gardens sharing a fence. That's what "adjoin" always describes.
To adjoin means to be directly next to something and share a common boundary — a wall, fence, or border — with no gap between the two things.
312:
Something is adjoining when it is directly next to something else and the two things physically share a common boundary — a wall, a fence, a border, or an edge — between them.

The word is doing two jobs at once. It tells you that two things are (1) right next to each other, and (2) literally touching each other along a shared dividing line. It is not enough for two things to be "nearby" or "close." They must be touching at that shared edge.

Imagine a hotel. Your room and the room next door share a wall. That is the shared boundary. Those are adjoining rooms. If your room is on the 3rd floor and another room is on the 5th floor, they are not adjoining — there is no shared wall between them.

Imagine two countries on a map, sharing a border. They are adjoining countries. If an ocean separates them, they are not adjoining.

Imagine two houses on a street, each with its own garden, and the two gardens share a fence. Those are adjoining gardens. A house three streets away is not adjoining, no matter how close it feels.

The shared boundary is always the key test. Ask yourself: "Do these two things touch each other along an edge?" If yes, adjoining fits.

"Please keep your voice down — the guests in the adjoining room will hear everything." (= the room next to yours, sharing your wall)

"The two adjoining countries agreed to open a new checkpoint at the border." (= countries sharing a physical border)

"She stepped through a small gate into the adjoining field." (= the field directly next to the one she was standing in, sharing a fence)

"The kitchen and the adjoining dining room made it easy to serve food quickly." (= the dining room is right next to the kitchen, sharing a wall)
An important nuance: shared boundary vs. shared access

In everyday life, "adjoining" often carries the feel of being able to pass from one space into the other — like adjoining hotel rooms that come with a connecting door between them. But access is not the actual requirement of the word. Two farms that share a fence line are adjoining farms even if there is no gate between them. Two countries are adjoining even if the border is sealed. What makes them adjoining is the shared boundary, full stop. Any access or connection between them is a bonus, not the definition.
How adjoining compares to similar words

Adjacent is the closest synonym and means almost the same thing — directly next to, sharing a boundary. In most everyday situations, you can swap one for the other. The difference is subtle: "adjacent" is occasionally used a little more loosely to mean "very near" even when things aren't perfectly touching, while "adjoining" almost always demands that genuine physical contact at a shared edge. "Adjoining" also has a stronger presence in formal, legal, and real estate language.

Neighboring is broader and more relaxed. Neighboring towns might be 15 miles apart with nothing shared between them. Adjoining is stricter — it requires that direct, touching boundary.

Connecting focuses on a passageway or link (a door, a corridor, a bridge), while "adjoining" focuses on the shared boundary itself. An adjoining room might or might not have a connecting door; a connecting room, by definition, has a passage to another.
Where you will most often encounter this word

Adjoining appears most heavily in real estate (an adjoining garage, an adjoining plot of land), architecture and interior design (an adjoining bathroom, an adjoining study), geography and politics (adjoining states, adjoining territories), hospitality (adjoining hotel rooms, frequently booked by families who want to be near each other but in separate rooms), and legal documents, where property boundaries must be described with precision.

Since you are learning the adjective form, it helps to know that the base verb is adjoin. You can say "Our backyard adjoins the park" (verb) — meaning our backyard shares a boundary with the park and touches it directly. The adjective "adjoining" simply takes that same idea and uses it to describe a noun: "the adjoining park." Understanding this connection makes the word much stickier in memory.
The one-line rule to remember it forever
Adjoining = right next to + sharing a boundary. If either piece is missing, the word does not apply.
313: To adjourn means to officially bring a formal gathering — such as a court session, a parliamentary debate, or a business meeting — to a close, either temporarily or permanently. The key idea is that this closing is deliberate and declared. A session doesn't simply "end" — it is adjourned by someone with the authority to do so.
Temporary vs. permanent — the most important nuance

When something is adjourned, it can go one of two ways:

Temporarily — The session is paused with a plan to continue later, at a specific time or date. "The judge adjourned the trial until next Thursday." This means the proceedings aren't over for good; they'll resume at the stated time.

Indefinitely (or permanently) — Sometimes a session is adjourned with no future date set. In formal contexts this is called adjourning sine die, meaning the session is simply over with nothing scheduled. Parliaments are often adjourned this way at the end of a legislative term.
A second meaning: adjourning to somewhere

There's an older, less formal use of adjourn that you may come across. When a formal gathering ends, the participants sometimes move together as a group to another location, and this movement can also be described as "adjourning to" that place.

"After the board meeting, the executives adjourned to the dining room for dinner."

Here it simply means they finished formal business and relocated as a group. This usage is more common in older or British writing, but you'll still encounter it.
How adjourn differs from similar words

This is important, because several words are close in meaning but are not the same.

Adjourn vs. Recess — A recess is a short pause within an ongoing session. A court might break for lunch and return an hour later; the session itself is still alive. An adjournment formally ends the session (even if a new session starts the next day). Think of recess as pressing pause, and adjournment as pressing stop.

Adjourn vs. Postpone — To postpone means to delay the start of something that hasn't happened yet. You postpone a meeting before it begins. You adjourn a meeting that is already in progress. Postpone points to the future; adjourn deals with something currently happening.

Adjourn vs. Cancel — Cancelling means something won't happen or is dropped entirely. Adjourning is a formal, structured close — it doesn't necessarily mean the matter is abandoned. A case can be adjourned and then resumed; a cancelled meeting is simply gone.

Adjourn vs. Suspend — Suspending proceedings often implies something unexpected interrupted the session, or that normal rules are being set aside for a reason. Adjournment is typically a routine, planned act of formally closing a session in the normal course of business.

Not everyone has the power to adjourn. In most formal settings, only the presiding officer — the judge, the chairperson, the speaker of a parliament — can declare a session adjourned. Sometimes the group itself can vote to adjourn.

The word is most at home in these settings: courts of law (judges adjourn hearings and trials), parliaments and legislatures (sessions are adjourned by the speaker or by vote), board and committee meetings (the chairperson adjourns once business is complete), and formal conferences (delegations adjourn international sessions).
The word in its different forms

• She adjourns the meeting. — present tense
  • The court was adjourned. — past tense; this passive form is the most common in everyday writing, because attention is on the meeting, not on who adjourned it
  • They are adjourning. — present continuous
  • The adjournment lasted two days. — noun form
  • After adjourning, the members left. — gerund (the -ing form used as a noun or describing an action)
A simple mental image to lock it in

Picture a judge in a courtroom. Everything is formal, structured, and official. When business is done — or needs to pause — the judge strikes a gavel and says: "Court adjourned." That single act is the formal declaration that what was officially opened is now officially closed, even if only for the day. That gavel strike is the essence of adjourn: a deliberate, authorized act of bringing a formal session to its conclusion.
314:
Imagine you're in an important meeting, and the chairperson says, "We can't finish everything today. Let's pause here and continue next Thursday." That official pause or postponement of a formal gathering is an adjournment.

In its simplest form: an adjournment is the formal suspension of a meeting, session, trial, or official proceeding — either to a later, fixed time, or with no set date to return.
The Two Things the Noun Can Refer To

The word "adjournment" can mean two slightly different (but closely related) things depending on how it's used in a sentence:

1. The act of officially suspending a session:

"The adjournment of the meeting was approved by a vote."

Here, "adjournment" refers to the decision or action of suspending the proceedings.

2. The period or interval during which the suspension lasts:

"During the adjournment, both sides consulted their lawyers."

Here, "adjournment" refers to the time gap between when proceedings were paused and when they resumed.

Both usages are correct and common. Context will almost always tell you which meaning is intended.
Where You'll Most Commonly See This Word

Adjournment is a formal word. You will encounter it most often in these settings:

Courts and Legal Proceedings
This is perhaps the most common context. A judge can grant an adjournment if a trial or hearing needs to be paused — perhaps a witness is unavailable, a lawyer needs more time to prepare, or new evidence has surfaced. The case doesn't disappear; it simply resumes at a later date.

"The defense attorney requested an adjournment to gather additional evidence."

Parliament and Government Legislatures
When a parliament, congress, or assembly formally ends its sitting for the day — or for a longer break — that is also an adjournment. Governments have official rules about how adjournments are called and voted on.

"Parliament voted in favour of an adjournment until the following week."

Business and Formal Meetings
Any formal meeting governed by rules (like a board meeting or a shareholders' meeting) can be adjourned. A motion to adjourn is typically the last business of such a meeting.

"At 4 PM, the chairperson moved for an adjournment."
What Makes an Adjournment Different from a Cancellation?

This is an important distinction.

  • A cancellation means the event is called off entirely — it won't happen.
  • An adjournment means the event is paused or postponed — the business is not finished, and it is generally expected to continue at some point.

An adjournment carries the idea that there is unfinished business that needs to be returned to. This is why it is a procedural tool rather than an ending.
The Special Case: Adjournment Sine Die (Indefinite Adjournment)

This is a critical concept to be aware of. Sometimes, proceedings are adjourned without setting a specific date to resume. This is called an adjournment sine die (a Latin phrase meaning "without a day"). In plain English: an indefinite adjournment.

This type of adjournment effectively ends the session permanently, because no return date is fixed. It is used when:

  • A legislative body's term has ended.
  • A case is closed with no prospect of continuing.
  • The matter at hand has been resolved and no further sessions are needed.

So, while most adjournments are temporary, an indefinite adjournment can signal a permanent end. The word "adjournment" alone, without "sine die," almost always implies that resuming is intended.

• An adjournment is always formal and official — it requires an authority (a judge, a chairperson, a speaker) to declare it, often following a vote or a recognized procedure.
  • It applies specifically to organized, formal proceedings — you wouldn't normally use this word for a casual get-together with friends.
  • It implies that the matter being discussed carries forward — it is not abandoned.
  • It can be for a set period (adjourned until 3 PM, adjourned until Monday, adjourned for two weeks) or indefinitely.

• "The judge granted the defense a two-week adjournment to review the new evidence."
  • "After a brief adjournment for lunch, the committee reconvened at 2 o'clock."
  • "The parliament declared an adjournment sine die at the end of its final session."
  • "A motion for adjournment was raised just before the vote could take place."
  • "The unexpected adjournment left reporters with little to report."

Since you're a learner, it helps to know the related forms so the word doesn't confuse you in different shapes:

  • Adjourn — the verb. "The court will adjourn at 5 PM." (To officially suspend or pause proceedings.)
  • Adjourned — the adjective/past tense. "The session was adjourned."
  • Adjournment — the noun you've just learned. The act of adjourning, or the period of suspension itself.

Adjournment is the formal, official suspension of a meeting, trial, or official session — either to a specified later time, or indefinitely — with the general understanding that the unfinished business will be continued.
315:
To adjudicate means to make an official, authoritative decision about a dispute, case, or competition — after carefully hearing and examining all sides of it.

Think of it this way: when two people disagree strongly and cannot resolve it themselves, they bring it to a neutral person or body with the power to settle it. That person listens to both sides, weighs the arguments and evidence, and then delivers a formal verdict. That entire act — of officially examining and then deciding — is adjudication.

It's not just any decision. It's a deliberate, structured, and authoritative one.

Understanding this word well means understanding what makes adjudication adjudication and not just "deciding":

1. Formality. Adjudication happens within a formal process — a courtroom, a competition panel, an arbitration hearing, an official committee. Your friend choosing which pizza topping is better is not adjudicating. A judge settling a legal dispute is.

2. A neutral authority. The person who adjudicates must have the recognized power or expertise to make a binding or official decision. They are not a participant in the dispute — they stand above it and rule upon it.

3. Hearing both sides first. Adjudication almost always implies that the decision-maker has listened and considered the arguments, claims, or performances before reaching a conclusion. It's not a snap judgment — it's a considered one.

In law and courts — this is the most common setting. A judge adjudicates a case between two parties (e.g., a plaintiff and a defendant). After hearing the evidence and arguments from both sides, the judge makes a ruling. Courts adjudicate everything from criminal trials to property disputes to contract disagreements.

"The Supreme Court was asked to adjudicate a case involving freedom of speech."

In competitions — expert judges are brought in to adjudicate music festivals, debate tournaments, science fairs, cooking competitions, and so on. They observe or listen to all participants and then decide who wins, who ranks where, and why.

"A panel of three industry experts adjudicated the national singing competition."

In formal disputes outside court — organizations, labor unions, government agencies, and businesses often adjudicate disputes without going to court. For example, an insurance company adjudicates a claim (decides whether it's valid and how much to pay), or an arbitrator adjudicates a conflict between an employer and employees.

"The arbitration board met to adjudicate the pay dispute between the airline and its pilots."

In government and administrative settings — government bodies often adjudicate applications and claims. Immigration courts adjudicate asylum cases. Benefits agencies adjudicate welfare claims.

"The immigration tribunal adjudicated his request for refugee status."

"Adjudicate" can be used in two ways:

With a direct object (transitive) — where you name the thing being decided upon:

  • "The committee adjudicated the dispute."
  • "The judge adjudicated the case."
  • "She adjudicated the competition."

Without a direct object, followed by "on" or "upon" (intransitive) — where you say what the decision is about:

  • "The tribunal was asked to adjudicate on the matter."
  • "He refused to adjudicate upon the conflict."

Both forms are correct — the choice usually depends on sentence flow and context.
Strength and Tone of the Word

This is an important word to understand well: adjudicate is a formal, serious word. You would not use it in casual conversation. It belongs in legal writing, official reporting, academic discussion, and formal contexts. Using it signals that the decision-making process involved structure, authority, and proper process — not just a quick judgment.

Knowing the whole family of this word helps you use it confidently:

  • Adjudication (noun) — the act or process of adjudicating. "The adjudication of the claim took three months."
  • Adjudicator (noun) — the person who adjudicates. "The adjudicator gave detailed feedback to each competitor."
  • Adjudicated (past tense/adjective) — "The adjudicated outcome surprised both parties."
  • Adjudicating (present participle) — "The panel is currently adjudicating the final round."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Since several words seem close in meaning, it's worth being precise:

  • Judge is broader and more casual. Anyone can "judge" something — even informally. Adjudicate always implies a formal process.
  • Decide is very general. Adjudicate is a specific kind of deciding — official, structured, and after due consideration of all sides.
  • Arbitrate is closely related and often overlaps with adjudicate. However, arbitration more specifically refers to settling disputes outside of court through a private process, while adjudication can happen in court or in any official forum.
  • Rule (on) focuses on the outcome (the ruling itself). Adjudicate encompasses the entire process — examining, considering, and then ruling.
One-Sentence Summary to Lock It In

To adjudicate is to officially and authoritatively examine all sides of a dispute, case, or competition, and then deliver a formal decision — typically done by a judge, arbitrator, or expert panel in a structured setting.
316:
An adjunct is something — or someone — that is added to a main thing but is not an essential or permanent part of it. It plays a supporting, secondary role. Without the adjunct, the main thing still works perfectly fine. The adjunct simply makes it more complete, more useful, or more effective.

Think of a car and a sunroof. The car drives without a sunroof. The sunroof is added on, enhances the experience, but is not essential to what a car fundamentally is. In the language of this word, the sunroof is an adjunct to the car.

Three qualities always define an adjunct. It is added to something else (it's not the original, central thing). It is subordinate (it serves the main thing, not the other way around). And it is non-essential (the main thing can exist and function without it).

In general use, you might hear sentences like "music is an adjunct to my workout" — meaning music is something added to the workout to enhance it, but the workout itself is the main event. Or "the new department serves as an adjunct to the main office" — meaning it assists and supports the central operation without being the core of it. Anywhere something is added on in a supporting, secondary capacity, the word "adjunct" fits.

This is one of the most precise and commonly tested uses of the word. In grammar, an adjunct is any word, phrase, or clause added to a sentence to provide extra information — but which is not grammatically required for the sentence to be complete or correct.

Consider: "She reads." That is already a complete, correct sentence. Now add some adjuncts: "She reads quietly, in her room, every evening." The words "quietly," "in her room," and "every evening" are all adjuncts. They tell us how, where, and when — but if you strip all of them away, the sentence "She reads" is still perfectly grammatical and meaningful. That is the hallmark of an adjunct: it can be removed without breaking the sentence.

Now compare that with something that truly is essential: "She placed the book on the shelf." Remove "on the shelf" and you get "She placed the book" — which feels incomplete and almost wrong. So here, "on the shelf" is not an adjunct; it's a required part of the sentence. This contrast is the clearest way to feel the difference.

An adjunct professor (or adjunct faculty member) is someone who teaches at a university or college but is not a permanent, full-time member of the institution. They are hired on a temporary or part-time basis — often just to teach specific courses — and don't have the same job security, benefits, or institutional standing as full-time, tenured professors. They are, in a sense, "added on" to the teaching staff to fill specific needs, without being core members of the faculty. This is probably the most widely encountered use of the word in everyday news and conversation.

Medicine uses "adjunct" frequently. An adjunct therapy or adjunct treatment is a secondary treatment added alongside the primary treatment to support or boost its effectiveness. For example, if a patient's main treatment is surgery, the doctor might recommend physiotherapy as an adjunct — it aids recovery but is not the central intervention. The primary treatment is the main thing; the adjunct is the supporting addition.
A Subtle but Important Point About Status

The word "adjunct" often carries a quiet implication of lesser standing. An adjunct professor earns less and has less security than a full professor. An adjunct feature in a product is secondary to the core features. However, this does not mean an adjunct is unimportant or ineffective — it simply means it is subordinate to something else. An adjunct therapy can be crucial to a patient's recovery. Adjuncts in a sentence can carry rich, vivid detail. The word is about position and role, not about worth.

No matter the context — grammar, academia, medicine, or everyday speech — the word "adjunct" always points to the same underlying idea: something added, something supportive, something that enhances the main thing without being the main thing itself. It is attached but not central, useful but not indispensable, present but secondary. Once you lock onto that core image of "a valuable addition that serves something greater than itself," you will recognize this word correctly in any sentence you encounter.
317:
An adjuration is a deeply solemn, serious appeal or command — one that carries extraordinary urgency and moral weight. It is not a casual request, not a polite ask, and not an ordinary order. It sits somewhere between a heartfelt plea and a binding command, charged with gravity and sincerity.

The single thing that makes an adjuration distinct from every other kind of appeal is this: it invokes something sacred, holy, or supremely important to give the request or command its binding force. The person making the adjuration essentially says, "I am asking you in the name of something you cannot ignore — God, truth, your soul, your oath."

The word adjuration is used in two closely related but distinguishable ways:

1. A solemn, earnest entreaty made by invoking a higher power

This is the most common use. When someone makes an adjuration in this sense, they are pressing another person with the deepest possible urgency — not just asking, but almost binding them morally by calling upon something sacred. The force of the appeal comes from what is invoked: God, a holy name, a sacred oath, conscience, or something the listener holds dear.

Think of it this way: if ordinary asking is a knock on a door, an adjuration is falling to one's knees at that door and saying, "I beg you in the name of God — you must answer me." There is desperation in it, but also authority.

2. A formal ritual command used to compel spiritual or supernatural forces

This is the older, more religious or ceremonial use. In religious rites, an adjuration is a set formula — a solemn charge — spoken to compel a spirit, a demon, or a divine force to act, stop, reveal, or depart. Exorcism prayers, for instance, are filled with adjurations. The speaker is not requesting the spirit to leave; they are commanding it, but doing so in the name of God or a holy authority that gives the command its power. Without invoking that authority, the command would carry no force.
What Makes It Feel Different from Similar Words

It helps to compare adjuration to nearby words:

  • A request is polite and optional. You can decline it.
  • A command has authority but doesn't necessarily carry spiritual or emotional gravity.
  • A plea is emotional and urgent but lacks the formal, invoking element.
  • An oath is a promise you make about your own behavior.
  • An adjuration combines the urgency of a plea, the seriousness of a command, and the binding weight of an oath — but it is directed outward at someone else, and it draws its power from invoking something greater than the speaker themselves.

The invoking element is the heart of it. Without that element — without the sense that something sacred or supremely binding is being called upon — it would just be a very strong request. With it, it becomes an adjuration.

Adjuration is a formal, elevated word. You will not hear it in everyday conversation. You will encounter it most often in:

  • Religious texts and scripture (it appears repeatedly in the Bible, for example, where priests, prophets, or individuals put someone under solemn oath by invoking God)
  • Historical literature and formal writing
  • Legal or ceremonial language where oaths and formal charges appear
  • Serious literary fiction where a character implores another with the utmost gravity

When you see the word, it signals that what is being described is not light or casual — it is a moment of maximum seriousness.
Concrete Examples to Fix the Meaning

Example 1 — The religious/ritual sense:
In the Gospel of Matthew, the high priest says to Jesus during his trial: "I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ." This is a classic adjuration. He is not simply asking. He is formally charging Jesus, in the name of God, to answer — invoking divine authority to make the demand binding and unavoidable.

Example 2 — The earnest entreaty sense:
A father on his deathbed, gripping his son's hand and saying, "I adjure you — swear to me before God that you will look after your mother and your brothers" — that is an adjuration. The dying man is pressing his son with every ounce of moral weight available to him, invoking God to make the appeal as binding as possible.

Example 3 — A slightly more literary use:
A character in a novel might write in a letter: "I send you this as my adjuration — by everything we once shared, by every promise you ever made me, do not let them destroy what we built." Even without naming God explicitly, the writer is invoking the sacred weight of shared memory and past promises to give their appeal its gravity.

An adjuration is a solemn, urgent appeal or command that draws its binding force from invoking something sacred, holy, or supremely authoritative — making it far more than an ordinary request and closer to a moral charge that the recipient cannot easily dismiss.
318: To adjure someone means to urgently and solemnly urge, appeal to, or command them to do — or not do — something. It is never a light or casual request. It always carries a sense of gravity, seriousness, and high stakes.

Imagine a moment where the stakes are extremely high — a deathbed scene, a courtroom, a last desperate conversation between two people. In those moments, saying "please" or "I'm asking you to" doesn't feel weighty enough. The speaker reaches for something stronger, something that binds the other person more deeply. That is when someone adjures.

When you adjure someone, you are not simply asking. You are making an appeal with everything you have — your authority, your moral weight, your desperation, or the sacredness of something like a vow, a name, or a bond. The word suggests that the speaker wants to make it as hard as possible for the other person to refuse — not through force, but through the sheer seriousness of the appeal.

Adjure carries two shades of meaning that often blend into each other:

1. To solemnly and earnestly beg or urge
This is a heartfelt, solemn plea. The speaker is appealing with deep seriousness.

"She adjured him not to throw his life away on this foolish decision."

2. To formally command or charge someone
This is more authoritative. The speaker has a position of power and is formally binding someone to an action.

"The judge adjured the witness to tell the whole truth."

In both senses, the key quality is identical: this is not an everyday request. It is earnest, weighty, and loaded with consequence.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is important because adjure has several close relatives, but none of them are quite the same:

  • Ask / request — purely neutral, no solemnity whatsoever.
  • Beg — shows raw desperation and emotion, but lacks the formal or sacred dimension.
  • Urge — suggests encouragement, but is too mild and lacks gravity.
  • Implore / entreat — these come closest. They are emotional, earnest appeals. But adjure adds an extra layer: it often invokes something sacred, authoritative, or binding — an oath, a name, a moral duty, a relationship — to reinforce the appeal.
  • Command / order — purely authoritative with no emotional or sacred weight. Adjure is different because it appeals to the other person's conscience, sense of honour, or feeling of obligation, rather than just issuing a directive.

The unique flavour of adjure is this combination: the urgency of pleading + the weight of authority or sanctity. It sits somewhere between a plea and a command.

One very common and important grammatical pattern with adjure is: adjure someone by something. This means the speaker is making the appeal in the name of — or anchored to — something the other person holds sacred or dear: God, an oath, a shared history, a deep bond.

"He adjured her by their years of friendship to reconsider."
"The priest adjured the congregation by the name of God to examine their hearts."

This "by something" pattern is one of the features that makes adjure distinctly itself. The appeal isn't floating in the air — it is grounded in something that gives it moral or sacred force.

Adjure always takes a person as its object — you adjure someone. After that, you typically use the infinitive form (to + verb) to say what you want them to do.

The full pattern looks like this:
adjure + [person] + (by something) + to do something

"I adjure you to keep this secret."
"He adjured her by all that was holy to stay."

Adjure is a formal word. You would never hear it in everyday small talk ("I adjure you to pass the salt"). It appears most naturally in:

  • Literary or religious writing — where the language is elevated and the stakes are high.
  • Legal or official settings — a judge formally adjuring a witness; a solemn oath being administered.
  • High-stakes dramatic moments in fiction — characters making desperate, binding appeals to each other.
  • Formal speeches or moral declarations — a leader adjuring a nation to rise to its responsibilities.

• "The dying queen adjured her successor to protect the people above all else."
  • "I adjure you, by everything we have shared, not to go down this path."
  • "The general adjured his soldiers to hold the line, whatever the cost."
  • "The prophet adjured the people to turn away from wrongdoing before it was too late."
  • "She adjured the court, in the name of justice, to consider the evidence carefully."

To adjure is to make a solemn, urgent, and deeply serious appeal to someone — urging or commanding them to do or refrain from doing something. It carries moral weight, often invokes something sacred or authoritative, and lives somewhere between a heartfelt plea and a formal command. It is the word you reach for when an ordinary request simply does not feel strong enough for what the moment demands.
319:
To adjust means to make a small, careful change to something so that it becomes more correct, more comfortable, or more suitable for a purpose.

Think of it this way: something is mostly fine, but not quite right. Adjusting it means you're fine-tuning it — nudging it toward the ideal state. You are not replacing it, rebuilding it, or fixing something that is broken. You are simply bringing it closer to where it needs to be.

A tailor adjusts your shirt — he takes it in a little at the sides. He isn't making a new shirt. He's making this one fit you better.
The Two Main Ways "Adjust" Is Used

1. You Adjust a Thing (You Change Something)

Here, "adjust" is about physically or practically changing an object, a setting, a plan, a number, or anything external — so that it works better or suits the situation better.

Examples:

  • She adjusted the brightness of her phone screen because the sunlight was too strong.
  • He adjusted his tie before walking into the meeting room.
  • The engineer adjusted the pressure in the machine so it wouldn't overheat.
  • The teacher adjusted the lesson plan after realizing the students needed more time.
  • Please adjust the volume — it's too loud.
  • The dentist adjusted the position of the brace.

In every case, notice: the thing existed and worked in some way, but a small, deliberate change made it more suitable.

2. You Adjust Yourself (You Adapt to Something New)

This is the second, equally important meaning. When a situation or environment is new or different, and you change your behavior, habits, feelings, or expectations to match it — you are adjusting.

This is almost always written as "adjust to" something.

Examples:

  • It took her several months to adjust to her new city.
  • Children usually adjust to a new school faster than their parents expect.
  • After his knee injury, he had to adjust to walking with a cane.
  • When I moved to a colder country, I found it hard to adjust to the weather.
  • He lost his job, and the whole family had to adjust to a tighter budget.

Here, "adjust" doesn't mean you are fixing yourself. It means you are responding to a changed reality by gradually changing how you live, think, or feel. The key idea is a process — it takes time, effort, or discomfort, and eventually things settle into a new normal.

The word "adjust" carries three quiet but important implications:

  1. The change is small or moderate, not total. If you are rebuilding something from the ground up, or making a massive transformation, "adjust" sounds wrong. You don't "adjust" a building — you renovate it. But you do adjust a single door that doesn't close properly.
  2. The change is intentional and purposeful. You're not randomly changing something — you are targeting a specific problem and correcting for it.
  3. The thing being adjusted was mostly already there. It just needed a little correction, alignment, or fine-tuning. A good analogy: if your car is running roughly, a mechanic might adjust the engine timing — not replace the engine.

Adjust vs. Fix
"Fix" implies something was broken or wrong. "Adjust" implies something was merely not perfectly suited yet.

  • You fix a broken tap. You adjust the water pressure.

Adjust vs. Change
"Change" is a broad word — it can mean anything from a tiny tweak to a complete overhaul. "Adjust" specifically means a small, targeted change.

  • You might change your entire career. But you adjust your schedule to make space for a new class.

Adjust vs. Adapt
"Adapt" and "adjust to" are very close in meaning when talking about people. But "adapt" often implies a bigger, more fundamental shift — sometimes even a change in identity or structure. "Adjust" is softer, smaller, and more everyday.

  • A species adapts over thousands of years. A person adjusts to a new routine within weeks.

Adjust vs. Tweak
"Tweak" means almost the same thing as adjust, but it is more informal and implies an even tinier change.

  • You adjust the recipe. You tweak it again after tasting it.
Common Collocations (Words That Naturally Go with "Adjust")

Knowing what words typically appear near "adjust" will help you use it naturally:

  • Adjust the settings / the temperature / the volume / the contrast
  • Adjust your expectations / your plans / your approach / your attitude
  • Adjust the mirror / the seat / the strap
  • Adjust to life / to change / to a new job / to the time zone
  • Adjust accordingly — this very common phrase means "to change in a way that responds suitably to a situation"
    • "We don't know yet how many guests are coming, but we'll adjust accordingly."

The adjective well-adjusted is commonly used to describe a person. It means someone who is emotionally healthy, stable, and capable of handling life's challenges without falling apart. Such a person has successfully managed to adjust to the realities of the world around them.

  • "Despite a difficult childhood, she grew up to be a confident and well-adjusted adult."

Its opposite, poorly adjusted, describes someone who struggles to cope or fit into their environment.

Core meaningTo make a small, careful, purposeful change so something works better or fits better
When used on things"Adjust the chair, the plan, the dosage, the settings"
When used on people"Adjust to a new place, routine, or situation" — meaning to slowly adapt
What it impliesSmall change, not total overhaul; intentional; improving fit or function

In one sentence: To adjust is to make a deliberate, small change — to a thing, a plan, or yourself — so that it better suits the situation it's in.
